## Paper

## Abstract

Lithium-ion battery (LIB) recycling is crucial for energy security, environmental sustainability, and economic viability, as the finite lifespan of LIBs results in a significant annual accumulation of spent units. However, effectively and precisely recovering valuable metal ions such as Li+, Mn2+, Ni2+ and Co2+ from complex LIB leaching solutions remains a major challenge. Here, we present a scalable electro-membrane crystallization-assisted general recycling (e-MCGR) technology for the selective and efficient recovery of those metal ions from LIB leaching solutions. By synergistically integrating electrochemical and electro-membrane technologies, our proposed technology incorporates four key configurations: selective membrane dual-stage distillation, bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization, membrane metal-complexing ex-situ crystallization, and membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization. We systematically analyze the metal-ion transfer kinetics of electro-membranes (ion selectivity and permeation rates) and the performance of electro-membrane crystallization systems (recovery rates and product purity), alongside evaluating energy consumption, economic viability, and environmental benefits. Our optimized e-MCGR process achieves a recovery of 95.5% for Li+, 99.5% for Mn2+, 83.1% for Ni2+, and 87.3% for Co2+, yielding high product purities of 99.9% for Li2CO3, 99.9% for Mn3O4, 99.5% for Ni(OH)2 and 92.5% for Co(OH)2. The e-MCGR technology demonstrates significant potential to reshape LIB recycling paradigms, aligning technological efficiency with energy, environmental and economic sustainability.

---

## Introduction

Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), the powerhouse of modern electronics, have been a global cornerstone to power billions of electronic devices1. They have undergone exponential and fast development in adding resilience to electrical grids with increasing contributions from intermittent sources2,3. By 2024, global LIB production reached approximately 3950 gigawatt-hours (GWh), with China contributing over 2677 GWh of this output, which represented over 65% of the global market share (Fig. 1a). Such rapid expansion of the LIB production underscores China’s success in reducing reliance on carbon-based energy while advancing renewable energy adoption (Supplementary Fig. 1). Unfortunately, the finite lifespan of these batteries (typically 2–9 years, around 500–3000 cycles) results in a substantial annual accumulation of spent batteries4. According to the data, the global generation of spent LIBs surged 1700 Kilotons (Kt) in 2024, with the volumes expected to rise further as demand grows (Supplementary Fig. 3). This escalating influx of spent batteries poses critical energy, economic, and environmental challenges, particularly in major economies with high LIB usage, such as China, the United States, European nations, Japan, and Korea (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 2).

The efficient recycling of spent batteries has become an imperative priority5–7. Among the complex composition of spent LIBs, the recovery of high-value metal ions, such as Li+, Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+, offers a potential opportunity for resource reclamation8,9. Typically, spent LIBs are dissolved in acidic solutions, followed by pH adjustment (~7) to obtain a leaching solution10, from which metal ions need to be recovered efficiently and precisely. To address these challenges, various approaches such as adsorption, ion exchange, solvent extraction, precipitation, or evaporative crystallization have been explored11–14. While some of these methods enable metal ion recovery, their limitations stem from imprecise separation and inefficient purification15,16. Thus, achieving metal ion recovery with both high recovery and high-purity products in a sustainable manner remains a significant hurdle. Additionally, most existing approaches focus narrowly on technical aspects, often overlooking system-level integration and sustainability17–19.

In recent decades, membrane technologies with tunable structures and functional groups have shown great promise as an efficient method for ion separation20–22. Among them, electrodialysis, by using electro-membranes, has emerged as a viable approach for recovering ion resources from diverse streams23–25. Advances in material science have led to the development of electro-membranes with tailored ion selectivity, enabling precise targeting of specific ions even in the presence of competing species with similar physicochemical properties26–30. However, ion transport across the electro-membranes is constrained by their ion-transfer kinetics (e-MK), resulting in trade-offs between ion selectivity and permeation rates13,31–33. Notably, recent research efforts have been directed toward combining electrochemical systems with crystallization to enhance metal ion recovery, resulting in the development of electrochemical crystallization. This approach enables simultaneous metal ion separation and crystal product generation24,34–36. Yet, a trade-off between the high ion recovery rate and product purity exists at the process scale37–39. To address this, hybridizing electrochemical systems with electro-membrane technology and crystallization technology (e-MC) offers a promising pathway for achieving metal ions with both high recoveries and high product purities. Previously, membrane technologies have relied on principles such as size exclusion, electrostatic interactions, and chemical affinity to achieve ion selectivity31,40–42. Although substantial progress has been made toward developing membranes with precise single-ion selectivity, their utility in real-world resource recovery remains limited by material constraints and has largely been tested only in isolated/single systems43–45. Furthermore, their applicability in LIB recycling has not been convincingly demonstrated42,46.

To bridge this gap, we propose an e-MC-assisted general recycling (e-MCGR) concept, which integrates mature membranes into a closed-loop and modular framework tailored for spent LIB recycling. The e-MCGR concept is designed to address both separation precision and practical applicability while maintaining high recovery and product purity. As illustrated in Fig. 2, the process begins with disassembly and acidic dissolution of spent LIBs, followed by pH adjustment (~7) to generate a representative leaching solution47. Valuable metals ions, such as Li+, Mn2+, Ni2+ and Co2+, are then selectively recovered through a three-part process: (i) separation of monovalent cations (Li+ and Na+) from divalent cations (Mn2+, Ni2+ and Co2+) through selective membrane dual-stage distillation; (ii), separation of monovalent cations from each other (separation Li+ and Na+) and Li+ crystallization via bipolar membrane in situ crystallization and (iii) selective recovery of Mn2+, Ni2+ and Co2+ by membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization and membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization. These processes enable the recovery of high-purity Li2CO3, Mn3O4, Ni(OH)2 and Co(OH)2. Despite the strategic importance of metal ion recovery from spent LIBs, no comprehensive study or design has yet explored a fully sustainable LIB recycling through this e-MCGR concept. Furthermore, the potential of LIB recycling to enhance energy security, environmental sustainability, and economic viability remains insufficiently explored. This e-MCGR presents an innovative framework and practical strategy for optimizing metal ion recovery, thereby addressing the challenges encountered in sustainable resource recovery from LIBs. Given the global scale of LIB development, this e-MCGR concept and approach contribute a holistic, scalable, and sustainable solution to address global challenges in LIB waste management and resource recovery.

---

## Results

Separation of monovalent cations from divalent cations
The e-MCGR starts with ultrafiltration (UF, Supplementary Table 6), where the organic pollutants in the feed are removed to minimize membrane clogging. Then the metal ions in the feed are concentrated using reverse osmosis (RO, Supplementary Table 6) before entering the ED cell due to low metal ion concentration in spent LIB leaching solutions (Fig. 2, Supplementary Table 7). Due to the unique thermodynamic and physical characteristics of metal ions, such as specific hydrated diameters and hydration energy (Supplementary Table 8), monovalent metal ions (Li+ and Na+) can be separated from multivalent metal ions (Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+). Recent advancements have enabled the use of commercial monovalent ion-selective electro-membranes, which operate based on mechanisms such as size exclusion and electrostatic repulsion (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 5). To efficiently recover those valuable metal ions, Li+ and Na+ are separated from Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+ through continuous selective electrodialysis. The separation is firstly evidenced by the change in color of the leaching solution (Fig. 3b), where the dark brown of the leaching solution is changed to a dark red solution containing Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+, while the solution containing only Li+ and Na+ is colorless.

To enhance separation efficiency, a multi-stage selective electrodialysis could be employed, but it is limited by practical constraints in metal ion recovery rates and the trade-offs in energy, economic, and environmental benefits48. Therefore, a more suitable two-stage selective electrodialysis configuration is designed here, termed as selective membrane dual-stage distillation (Supplementary Fig. 6). The impact of current density on e-MK is evaluated by using three current densities (i.e., 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 mA cm−2). In the first-stage selective electrodialysis at operating condition of 1.0 mA cm−2 with 4 L of leaching solutions in the feed chamber, the concentrations of Li+ and Na+ increase in the recovery chamber (Fig. 3c). In this configuration, multivalent metal ions (Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+) are rejected by the selective membranes, while Li+ and Na+ readily permeate (Supplementary Fig. 7). However, residual Mn2+ (0.06 g L−1), Ni2+ (0.06 g L−1) and Co2+ (0.07 g L−1) mixed with amounts of Na+ (0.04 g L−1) and Li+ (0.14 g L−1) in transitional chambers necessitate further separation due to the limited selectivity of commercial membranes. Thus, the 2 L transitional solutions (in transitional chamber-1 and transitional chamber-2) from the first-stage selective electrodialysis are fed into the second-stage selective electrodialysis for additional separation (Fig. 3d). This selective membrane dual-stage distillation configuration proves optimal for separating Li+ and Na+ from Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+. With the combination of first-stage operating at 1 mA cm−2 and second-stage at 0.5 mA cm−2, this dual-stage distillation achieves the highest accumulative recoveries of 96.5% for Li+ and 96.4% for Na+, while completely rejecting Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+ (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Fig. 8).

Effectively, the transport of metal ions from the feed chamber to the recovery chamber is governed by e-MK and reflected by voltage change (Supplementary Fig. 9). Regardless of stages or operating conditions, the e-MK is the critical factor for determining metal ion selectivity, permeation rate, and ultimately, recovery and purity. Although additional stages could enhance metal ion recovery purity, they lead to higher losses of Li+ and Na+ in the transitional chamber and higher energy consumption. Thus, the selective membrane dual-stage distillation technology strikes an optimal balance for separating monovalent cations (Li+ and Na+) and multivalent cations (Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+) with current membranes technologies.

A comprehensive evaluation of energy consumption, economic profitability, and environmental benefits is conducted for this selective membrane dual-stage distillation configuration (Supplementary Fig. 10). With this optimized configuration, most of this energy is consumed by metal ion transport in membranes. For this selective membrane dual-stage distillation, key metrics, such as energy consumption (EC), energy cost (Ce), investment cost (Ci), Li+ recovery cost (CLi), monovalent metal ion recovery rate (Rm), and purity of recovered Li+ (PLi), are analyzed and summarized (Supplementary Fig. 10 and Supplementary Table 9). For the first-stage selective electrodialysis, the impact of current density on separation kinetics is evaluated at 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 mA cm−2. At 1.0 mA cm−2, the system demonstrated the lowest energy cost (1.24 $ kg−1), investment cost (3.78 $ kg−1), and the energy consumption (11.83 kWh kg−1), along with the highest monovalent cation recovery rate (87.7%), compared to 66.8% and 60.5% at 2.5 and 5.0 mA cm−2, respectively (Fig. 3f). To further enhance Li+ recovery, transitional solutions from the first-stage selective electrodialysis are processed in a second-stage selective electrodialysis operated at a lower current density (0.5 mA cm−2). Based on the operating conditions and the expenditure per 1 kg of LiCl recovery, this configuration achieves around 96.5% recovery of monovalent metal ions (Li+ and Na+), with an energy cost of 2.73 $ kg−1, investment cost of 13.25 $ kg−1, and energy consumption of 15.97 kWh kg−1 (Fig. 3g). This initial separation of monovalent and multivalent cations is essential for efficient resource recovery, both technologically and in terms of energy, economic, and environmental reasons. While selective membrane dual-stage distillation technology achieves a high separation efficiency, current commercial membranes are limited by their metal ion throughput. In addition, they suffer from severe membrane scaling (Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12). On the one hand, this scaling can be attributed to the inherent poor anti-scaling properties of commercial electro-membrane. On the other hand, water splitting may occur on the CIMS surface as most divalent ions are electrostatically repelled and cannot serve as current carriers. The resulting shortage of charge carriers induces forced dissociation of water into H⁺ and OH⁻, with OH⁻ reacting with accumulated metal ions to form insoluble hydroxide precursors that deposit on the membrane surface (Supplementary Fig. 13).

Recovery of Li+ and Na+
Following the initial separation configuration, the recovered feed contains only monovalent metal ions (Li+ and Na+), yet the lack of highly Li+-selective electro-membranes poses a significant challenge, and current electrodialysis cannot achieve crystallization. Our innovative approach offers a solution that enables simultaneous metal ion separation and crystallization of Li2CO3. Typically, CO2 is captured by reacting with OH−, a method commonly employed for carbon capture and storage, and utilized as a carbonate source. Leveraging the bipolar membrane electrodialysis, an in situ crystallization configuration is developed to separate Li+ from Na+ while generating high-purity Li2CO3 crystals (Supplementary Fig. 14). In this system, CO2 is captured via a membrane contactor (Supplementary Fig. 15) and reacts with the OH− generated in situ by the bipolar membrane (chemical reaction pathways are detailed in Supplementary Fig. 16). This hybridization of bipolar membrane and in situ crystallization technologies ensures Li+ capture, CO2 utilization, and Li2CO3 production (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 17).

Figure 4b illustrates the mechanisms of the bipolar membrane in situ crystallization process, culminating in the formation of white powder products. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) reveals that the precipitated powders exhibit a regular octahedral crystal structure with an average diameter of 4 μm (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 18). The element mapping confirms the homogeneous distribution of C and O within the particles (Supplementary Fig. 18). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) further vindicates the crystal purity and shows atomic percentages of 29.9% Li and 45.1% O, with less than 0.1% Na (Fig. 4d). High-resolution XPS spectra of C1s and O1s confirm the presence of C=O and C–O bonds in those generated crystals (Supplementary Fig. 19). X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis further confirms that all the crystals are Li2CO3, demonstrating a high product purity (Fig. 4e).

The temporal evolution of Li+ and Na+ concentrations in the bipolar membrane in situ crystallization configuration is shown in Fig. 4f. At an optimized current density of 5 mA cm−2, both Li+ and Na+ in the feed chamber decrease to an extremely low value. In the recovery chamber, the Li+ initially increases and then decreases to 0.1 g L−1 due to the in situ crystallization of Li2CO3 (reaction mechanisms are detailed in Supplementary Fig. 17). This process yields Li2CO3 crystals with >99.9% purity (Fig. 4g). Without in situ crystallization, >99.0% of both Li+ and Na+ would be recovered (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 20). With this optimized configuration, >98.0% of Li+ is recovered from the leaching solution (achieves a recovery of 95.5% for Li+ in the whole process), and produces Li2CO3 with >99.9% purity. Additionally, the NaOH (>97.5% recovery, >95% purity) is recovered and reused as a basic solution in subsequent membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization as well as membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization configurations (Supplementary Fig. 21). High-purity HCl is generated for spent LIB dissolution and subsequent systems for divalent cation recovery.

This bipolar membrane in situ crystallization system not only generates high-purity Li2CO3 but also provides significant energy, economic, and environmental benefits. The recovered Li2CO3, NaOH, and HCl mitigate environmental pollution of discharged metal ions and safety risks associated with high metal ion concentrations while offering valuable ion resources for industrial applications. Measuring by economic efficiency of per $ kg−1 Li2CO3, as shown in Fig. 4h, the economic analysis reveals that the primary costs are energy consumption (1.10 $ kg−1 Li2CO3) and investment (membranes: 1.68 $ kg−1 Li2CO3, maintenance: 0.43 $ kg−1 Li2CO3). Given the current market price of Li2CO3 (24.00 $ kg−1), the system yields a profit of around 20.79 $ kg−1 Li2CO3 (Supplementary Tables 10 and 11). Beyond the Li2CO3 profits, this configuration also generates NaOH and HCl for supporting other LIB recycling configurations, along with environmental benefits such as CO2 fixation and zero liquid discharge. Despite those advantages, the system faces limitations of the current electro-driven membranes due to the low ion throughput and poor anti-scaling properties (Supplementary Fig. 22 and Fig. 23). Future work should focus on improving electro-membrane performance to enhance the metal ion throughput and mitigate electro-membrane issues that enable more efficient and sustainable LIB recycling.

Recovery of Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+
The tandem leaching streams from the selective membrane dual-stage distillation system contain Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+, which are extracted as valuable metals from the black mass obtained after precise dismantling and separation of spent LIBs. To recover those metal ions, the membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization, as well as membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization configurations, are developed, as illustrated in Fig. 5a. These systems exploit differential coordination behavior of Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+ to ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) and the extractant Cyanex 272 to selectively recover Mn3O4, Ni(OH)2, and Co(OH)2, respectively (Fig. 5b). According to coordination capacity to the EDTA complexing agent, in the membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization configuration, Ni2+ and Co2+ exhibits significantly higher coordination capacity with EDTA than Mn2+, thus forming [EDTA-Ni]2− (KNi = 2.51 × 1018) and [EDTA-Co]2− (KCo = 2.82 × 1016) (Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25). In contrast, Mn2+ exhibits a significantly lower coordination capacity with EDTA (KMn = 7.76 × 1013). Consequently, Mn2+ migrates to the recovery chamber as the experiment progresses (Supplementary Fig. 26f). A small amount of Ni2+ and Co2+ is also recovered along with Ni2+ when the molar ratio of EDTA to Ni+Co at 1, due to the incomplete complexation (Supplementary Figs. 26d, e). As the molar ratio of EDTA to Ni+Co increases to 1.05, no extra Ni2+ and Co2+ ions are observed in the recovery chamber, and Mn2+ approaches the highest recovery. However, a further increase in the molar ratio to 1.15 significantly decreases the recovery efficiency of Mn2+ due to the formation of Mn[EDTA]2−. Considering the higher recovery of Mn2+, the molar ratio of EDTA to Ni+Co is optimized at 1.05. With the extra-added H+, which is supplied from the bipolar membrane in situ crystallization, [EDTA-Ni]2− and [EDTA-Co]2− de-coordinate with EDTA, and the subsequent separation is carried out in the membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization configuration. Based on the higher affinity capacity to Cyanex 272, the Co2+ is more likely to form complex Co(Cyanex 272)2 and remain in the solution (Supplementary Figs. 27 and 28). Meanwhile, the Ni2+ migrates to the recovery chamber under the electrical field and is finally recovered as the green crystal of Ni(OH)2 (Fig. 5cii). With temporal control, the pink Co(OH)2 is finally obtained from the extracted chamber of the membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization system (Fig. 5ciii).

SEM imaging reveals distinct crystal morphologies with uniform elemental distribution for Mn, Ni, and Co, respectively (Fig. 5d). Various specific crystal structures with different diameters and high homogeneity of the elements’ distribution can be observed from those images. The XPS spectra results confirm high purity (>99.5%) of all obtained metal ion products (Fig. 5e), with high-resolution spectra validating bonding environments of Mn, Ni, and Co, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 29-31). The XRD analysis confirms phase-purity of the Mn3O4, Ni(OH)2, and Co(OH)2, respectively, with no other impurity peaks in each of the XRD spectra (Fig. 5f). The temporal evolution of Ni2+, Co2+. and Mn2+ concentrations in each chamber are measured using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES). In the membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization configuration (Fig. 5g), the Ni2+ and Co2+ form [EDTA-Ni]2− and [EDTA-Co]2− and migrate to the Ni & Co collect chamber in the anode side, while Mn2+, which remains uncomplexed, transports toward the cathode into the Mn recovery chamber. Then [EDTA-Ni]2− and [EDTA-Co]2− are decomplexed using 2.0 M H2SO4, the collected Ni and Co solution is used in the next membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization configuration (Fig. 5h). In the first 10 h, the Co2+ accumulates in the co-extraction chamber as the Co2+ complexes with Cyanex 272, forming non-charged Co(Cyanex 272)2, while positively charged Ni2+ migrates to the recovery chamber. After 10 h, Co(Cyanex 272)2 is dissociated into Co2+, which is transported to the recovery chamber later.

In the membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization system, with the optimized current density of 5 mA cm−2, the results reveal more than 99.5% Mn2+ recovery, and yield Mn3O4 with purity higher than 99.9% (Fig. 5i). Residual [EDTA-Ni]2− and [EDTA-Co]2− are retained in the collection chamber, ensuring fresh water reclamation and zero waste discharge. In the membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization configuration, with optimized operating conditions, Ni2+ and Co2+ are recovered with recoveries of higher than 83.1% and 87.3%, generating the final products of Ni(OH)2 and Co(OH)2 with more than 99.5% and 92.5% purity, respectively (Fig. 5i).

The recovery of high-purity Mn3O4, Ni(OH)2, and Co(OH)2 not only addresses the heavy metal ion pollution but also delivers significant economic benefits. Taking Mn3O4 as an example, in the membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization configuration, taking the economic efficiency per $ kg−1 Mn3O4, the energy consumption and investment costs are 1.30 and 1.02 $ kg−1 Mn3O4, respectively (Fig. 5j). With a market price of ~9.00 $ kg−1 Mn3O4, this configuration yields profits of 6.68 $ kg−1 Mn3O4 (Supplementary Table 12). In the membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization configuration, measured by economic efficiency of per $ kg−1 [Ni(OH)2 + Co(OH)2] (with the mole ratio of 47:53), the energy consumption and investment costs are 1.89 and 1.86 $ kg−1 [Ni(OH)2 + Co(OH)2], respectively (Fig. 5j). Given market prices of >14 $ kg−1 for Ni(OH)2 and >18 $ kg−1 for Co(OH)2, this system brings a profit at least 12.37 $ kg−1 [Ni(OH)2 + Co(OH)2] (Supplementary Table 13). Compared to the mainstream technologies for Li recovery, the e-MCGR technology not only achieves a lower overall cost but also offers distinct profit advantages (Supplementary Table 14). Besides these energy consumptions, the extra NaOH and HCl are supplied and reused from the bipolar membrane in situ crystallization system. The EDTA and the Cyanex 272 are recycled in membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization and membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization systems, which minimize reagent consumption and enhance the system’s circularity. Considering the recovery rate of those metal ions, the profits could be improved when using the electro-driven membrane with high metal ion transport capacity in this configuration. Despite its energy, economic, and environmental advantages, those systems face challenges, particularly mineral scaling on electro-membranes, which limits metal ion throughput and recovery efficiency (Supplementary Fig. 32). To address these limitations, future efforts should focus on designing electro-membranes with higher ion transport capacity and enhanced anti-scaling properties. A fundamental study in advancing the understanding of metal ion crystallization kinetics in electro-membrane systems is essential to optimize recovery processes.

Recovery of metal ions from real LIBs leachate
The e-MCGR process for efficient LIBs recycling is further validated using real leachate from spent NMC111 cathode material (Fig. 6a). In the first-stage selective electrodialysis, operated at a current density of 1.0 mA cm−2, the CIMS membranes effectively reject multivalent metal ions (Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+) and permeate monovalent metal ions (Na+ and Li+). Thus, the concentrations of Li+ and Na+ increase to 1.08 g L−1 and 3.73 g L−1 in the recovery chamber, respectively (Fig. 6b). The residual solutions from the transitional chambers (in both transitional chamber-1 and transitional chamber-2) in the first-stage selective electrodialysis are then fed into the second-stage selective electrodialysis for further separation (Fig. 6c). This selective membrane dual-stage distillation configuration achieves accumulative recovery of 93.9% for Li+ and 89.1% for Na+, while completely rejecting Mn2+, Ni2+ and Co2+. This process demonstrates a low energy cost (1.56 $ kg−1), investment cost (7.08 $ kg−1), and energy consumption (14.87 kWh kg−1) (Supplementary Table 15).

Subsequent bipolar membrane in situ crystallization process recovers 96.6% Li+ from the leaching solution and produces Li2CO3 with > 99.9% purity (Fig. 6d, e). XPS analysis confirm the product’s composition, showing atomic percentages of 32.2% Li, and 39.6% O, with others less than 0.3% (Fig. 6f). The high purity of 99.9% was further verified by XRD analysis (Fig. 6g). The economic analysis reveals that the primary costs are energy consumption (0.72 $ kg−1 Li2CO3) and investment cost (2.12 $ kg−1 Li2CO3). Given the current market price of Li2CO3 (24.00 $ kg−1), the system yields a profit of around 21.16 $ kg−1 Li2CO3 (Supplementary Table 16). Moreover, 97.7% NaOH with 96.7% purity is recovered from the bipolar membrane in situ crystallization process.

In membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization, due to its lower coordination capacity with EDTA, Mn2+ migrates to the recovery chamber (Fig. 6h). In a separate membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization step, Ni2+ migrates to the recovery chamber and is recovered as Ni(OH)2 by adding NaOH (Fig. 6i). With temporal control, the pink Co(OH)2 is subsequently obtained from the extraction chamber. The membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization proves optimal for maximizing the recovery rate and product purity for all transition metals (Fig. 6j). The XPS spectra results confirm high purity (>92.0%) of all obtained metal ion products (Fig. 6k). The XRD analysis confirms the generation of Mn3O4 (Fig. 6l). The energy consumption and investment costs are 1.42 and 1.46 $ kg−1 Mn3O4, respectively. With a market price of ~9.00 $ kg−1 Mn3O4, this configuration yields profits of 6.12 $ kg−1 Mn3O4 (Supplementary Table 17). XRD analysis confirmed the phase-purity of the recovered Ni(OH)2 and Co(OH)2 (Fig. 6m, n). The process achieved an 80.1% recovery of Ni(OH)2 with 99.3% purity and, with temporal control, a 95.6% recovery of pink Co(OH)2 with 92.2% purity. The combined energy consumption and investment costs for recovering Ni(OH)2 + Co(OH)2 are 1.61 and 1.93 $ kg−1 [Ni(OH)2 + Co(OH)2], respectively. Given market prices of >14 $ kg−1 for Ni(OH)2 and >18 $ kg−1 for Co(OH)2, this system brings a profit of 12.58 $ kg−1 [Ni(OH)2 + Co(OH)2] (Supplementary Table 18).

## Methods

Pretreatment
The suspended solids in the feed are removed by using ultrafiltration (UP150 membrane) at an operating pressure of 0.01 MPa. Then the permeate is concentrated using reverse osmosis (RO, BW30 membrane) at an operating pressure of 1.5 MPa.

Configurations in the e-MCGR process
All experimental configurations described herein are conducted using a single, consistently prepared complex feed batch (the composition is shown in Supplementary Table 7) to ensure comparability and integration across the e-MCGR process. This batch simulated real LIB leachate is used sequentially across all experimental stages without intermediate reconstitution (Supplementary Table 19). The integrated design of the e-MCGR process comprises:

i. Selective membrane dual-stage distillation configuration: This configuration employs two sequential selective electro-membrane stacks to separate monovalent metal ions (Li+ and Na+) from the divalent metal ions (Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+). In the first-stage selective electro-membrane stack (Supplementary Fig. 6), the membranes are arranged as: anode / bipolar membrane (BM) / AMX (commercial anion exchange membrane) × 3 / CIMS (commercially monovalent cation exchange membrane) × 3 / bipolar membrane (BM) / cathode (Supplementary Table 20). The effective area per membrane is 0.0189 m2. Four chambers (feed, transitional-1, transitional-2, recovery) are connected to containers holding 2 L simulated LIB leaching solution in the feed chamber and 0.5 L deionized water in the other chambers. The operational parameters of the current densities are tested at 1 mA cm−2, 2.5 mA cm−2, and 5 mA cm−2. The electric current of the electro-membrane stack is supplied by a stabilized power supply. In order to further distill Li+ and Na+ from transitional chambers (transitional chamber-1 and transitional chamber-2) of the first stage, the second-stage selective electro-membrane stack is developed (Supplementary Fig. 6), and the electro-membrane stack arrangement is anode / BM / AMX × 2 / CIMS × 2 / BM / cathode. Three chambers in the electro-membrane stack consist of the feed chamber, the transitional chamber, and the recovery chamber. For those chambers, 1 L of residual solution from the first-stage transitional chambers is introduced into the feed chamber of the second-stage stacks, and the transitional and recovery chambers are initially fed with 0.5 L of deionized water. The current density of the electro-membrane stack is 0.5 mA cm−2. The refined Li+ and Na+ from the recovery chamber are then directly used as feed for the subsequent bipolar membrane in situ crystallization (ii) to separate Li+ from Na+.

ii. Bipolar membrane in situ crystallization configuration: In this configuration, the electro-membranes are stacked between anode and cathode in a sequence of the anode / BM / AMX / commercial cation exchange membrane (CMX) / BM / cathode (Supplementary Fig. 13), forming three chambers, including the feed chamber, the acid chamber, and the base chamber. Specifically, 1 L monovalent metal ions solution (Li+ and Na+) from the recovery chambers of configuration (i) is used as the initial feed, and 0.5 L of deionized water is fed to the acid and base chambers. The electric current of this electro-membrane stack is 5 mA cm−2, which is supplied by a direct current-stabilized power supply. To avoid Na+ impurities in Li2CO3 (caused by Na2CO3 co-precipitation) and capture the CO2 from industry, CO2 gas is introduced into the base chamber as a carbonate source, at a constant flow rate of 50 mL min−1 (Supplementary Fig. 14). During the reaction, CO2 dissolves into the solution and subsequently forms carbonate species. The Li2CO3 crystals will be crystallized in the base solution, followed by Li2CO3 recovery with the UP150 membrane.

CO2 + 2OH− ⇌ CO32− + H2O
Then, Li2CO3 crystallization occurs as
CO32− + 2Li+ ⇌ Li2CO3 (Ksp = 8.15 × 10−4)
Overall, the reaction is
2OH− + CO2 + 2Li+ ⇌ Li2CO3 ↓ + H2O

iii. Membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization configuration: Here, the membrane sequence is: anode / CMX / AMX / CMX / AMX / cathode (Supplementary Fig. 19), with three chambers: the feed, complexing, and the recovery chamber. The residual divalent metal-rich solution remaining after configuration (i) serves as the feed for this configuration. Herein, 3.0 L mixtures of Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+ are introduced into the feed chamber, and 0.5 L of deionized water is fed into the complexing and recovery chambers. The feed solution is further treated with the EDTA-4Na salt in the feed container. When the [EDTA]4− forms complex anions with Ni2+ and Co2+, with the EDTA’s differential coordination capacities (KNi > KCo ≫ KMn), the Mn2+ is separated from Ni2+ and Co2+ using this membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization system,

Ni2+ + EDTA4− ⇌ [EDTA-Ni]2− KNi = 2.51 × 1018
Co2+ + EDTA4− ⇌ [EDTA-Co]2− KCo = 2.82 × 1016
Mn2+ + EDTA4− ⇌ [EDTA-Mn]2− KMn = 7.76 × 1013

For the decomplexation, EDTA complexes are dissociated by adding 2.0 M HCl until pH < 0.5. To recover metal ions, Mn2+ in the recovery chamber is precipitated as Mn(OH)2 by using 1.0 M NaOH. Both the acid and base used here are provided by configuration (ii).

Mn2+ + 2OH− ⇌ Mn(OH)2 ↓
Then, the Mn(OH)2 is oxidized to black Mn3O4 crystals
6Mn(OH)2 + O2 ⇌ 2Mn3O4 ↓ + 6H2O

Membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization configuration: Connecting with the membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization configuration, this stack uses: anode / AMX / CMX / CMX / AMX / cathode (Supplementary Fig. 19). In this system, the membrane stack contains three containers, which connect with the feed chamber, the Co-extraction chamber, and the Ni-recovery chamber. The containers are initially fed with 0.5 L mixed Ni2+ and Co2+ solution from the membrane metal-complexing ex situ crystallization system, 0.5 L extraction solution (50% saponified Cyanex 272 in kerosene), and 0.5 L deionized water, respectively. The electric current of the complexation electrodialysis stack is tested at 5 mA cm−2. Due to the Cyanex 272 preferentially binds Co2+, it enables efficient Ni2+ and Co2+ separation. In this process, the Co2+ is extracted by Cyanex 272, which forms a stable complex with Cyanex 272 in the extraction chamber.

Co2+ + 2Cyanex 272 ⇌ Co(Cyanex 272)2 + 2H+
Then, the uncomplexed Ni2+ migrates to the Ni-recovery chamber under the electric field. The Ni2+ is precipitated as Ni(OH)2 with the usage of 1.0 M NaOH (supplied from the bipolar membrane in situ crystallization system).

Ni2+ + 2OH− ⇌ Ni(OH)2 ↓
With temporal crystallization of Ni2+, 2.0 M HCl is added to the feed chamber to release Co2+ from Cyanex 272,
Co(Cyanex 272)2 + 2H+ ⇌ Co2+ + 2Cyanex 272
Then, these Co2+ migrate to the Co-recovery chamber under the electric field and precipitate as Co(OH)2 with the usage of 1.0 M NaOH.

Co2+ + 2OH− ⇌ Co(OH)2 ↓

Validation of the e-MCGR process using real LIBs wastewater
To validate the practical feasibility of the e-MCGR process, real wastewater from spent ternary LIBs is used as feed. The spent ternary LIBs, sourced from a technology company’s power bank, are used as the primary raw materials. First, 0.4 g of waste NMC111 cathode material is leached in 4.0 M HCl at 80 °C for 6 h. The resulting leachate is subjected to the same pretreatment sequence as described in the “Pretreatment” section, namely ultrafiltration (UP150 membrane, 0.01 MPa) to remove organic impurities, followed by RO (BW30 membrane, 1.5 MPa) to concentrate the solution. The concentrated leachate, now enriched in Li⁺, Na⁺, Mn²⁺, Ni²⁺, and Co²⁺, is directly used as the feed for the e-MCGR process, without reconstitution or modification, to ensure a one-to-one comparison with the results obtained from the simulated LIB leachate.

Characterization methods
The chemical composition and bonding states of the recovered crystals are analyzed by using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; AXIS Ultra DLD, Shimadzu, Japan). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Sirion 200, FEI, USA) coupled with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS; INCA X-Act, USA) is employed to assess crystal morphology, surface roughness, and elemental distribution. The crystal phase identification is performed through X-ray diffractometry (XRD; XRD-6100, Shimadzu, Japan) using Cu-Kα radiation (λ=1.5 Å). Metal ion concentrations are quantified by using Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES; Avio 500, PerkinElmer, USA). The properties of ion exchange membranes used in the study are shown in Supplementary Table 12.

Evaluation methods
Technological analysis. Metal ion selectivity (P) is a parameter that is used to illustrate membrane ion selectivity. Compared to other metal ions (Mz+), the target metal ion selectivity can be calculated as
P = (Ttarget / Tother) / (Ctarget / Cother) * (Jtarget / Jother) (1)
Where Ttarget and Tother are the transport numbers of target metal ions and other metal ions. c (mol L−1) is the concentration of metal ions. J (mol m−2 s−1) is the metal ion permeation rate, which is used to illustrate ion transport capacity, and can be calculated as
J = (V * dc) / (S * dt) (2)
Where V (L) is the volume of solution, and S (m2) is the membrane area. The product recovery rate (R, %) is calculated by,
R = (mt / m) (3)
where mt (g) is the mass of precipitate recovered at time t, and m (g) is the theoretical maximum precipitate mass.
The equation of total suspended solids measurement, which is the crystal yield (Y, g L−1),
Y = mcry / Vbrine (4)
where mcry is the mass of dried crystals, and Vbrine (L) is the volume of feed wastewater.

Energy, economic, and environmental analysis. In this e-MCGR process, the specific energy consumption (E, kWh kg−1) is calculated by,
E = (∫0t Ut * I dt) / (Ct * Vt * Mt) (5)
where Ut (V) is the electro-membrane stack voltage, I (A) is the current, Vt (L) is the volume of solution, Ct (mol L−1) is the concentration, and Mt (g mol−1) is the molecular mass. More data on energy, economics, and the environment on this e-MCGR technology are analyzed and summarized in the Supplementary Information.

Data availability
The data generated in this study are provided in the article and its Supplementary Information. Visualization and figure preparation are carried out using Origin 8, Microsoft PowerPoint 2021, and Microsoft Excel 2021. Source data are provided with this paper.

This study introduces a modular and innovative electro-membrane crystallization-assisted general recycling (e-MCGR) platform for spent lithium-ion batteries. The configurations enable efficient recovery of high-purity metal products while minimizing chemical waste through the reuse of NaOH, HCl, and recycling of EDTA/Cyanex 272. ### Reviewer 3

Zhao and his colleagues reported a combined electro-membrane crystallization process for spent lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) recycling, termed e-MCGR technology. The proposed technology incorporated four core modules: selective membrane dual-stage distillation, bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization, membrane metal-complexing ex-situ crystallization, and membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization. However, similar individual module technologies have been proposed by peers for the recycling of lithium and other metallic elements from LIB streams (AIChE J. 68(2022), 17710; Nature Water 1(2023) 547–554; Chemical Engineering Journal 348(2018) 952–959; Resources, Conservation & Recycling 178 (2022) 106076; et al.). The novelty of this system is not clear because this article merely conceptually integrates these modular technologies. Furthermore, the above modules were studied separately in this manuscript, resulting in weak interconnectivity among them and insufficient comprehensive examination of the overall practical feasibility of the integrated technology. Additionally, the discussion on selective electrodialysis, electro-driven membrane in-sit crystallization and metal-extracting crystallization was insufficient, with some principal explanations containing scientific errors. The research results are insufficient to demonstrate the practical feasibility of the proposed e-MCGR technology. Therefore, this paper is not suitable for publication in Nature Communications. The detailed comments are as follows.
1. The LIB leaching solution used in this article should be a simulated solution prepared based on the ion composition of an actual LIB leaching solution. The authors should use the actual waste LIB leaching solution to verify the effectiveness of the technology. In particular, the manuscript and the supplementary information did not provide water quality data for the LIB solution used, which is essential for evaluating the work carried out throughout the manuscript.
2. The structure and content organization of the manuscript should be revised carefully to enhance its readability:
(1) The discussion in lines 123-133 of the Results and Analysis section focuses on the importance of e-MCGR system development, which aligns more appropriately with the Introduction. Please justify this arrangement.
(2) An in-depth theoretical analysis on the ion sieving mechanism of monovalent selective ion membranes (CIMS) is lacking.The authors repeatedly describe four ion sieving mechanisms (Lines 123-125, Lines161-164 and Figure S5) but fail to link these mechanisms to the experimental results. Since typically only 1–2 mechanisms are functionally relevant in conventional CIMS applications, specify the primary mechanism governing the CIMS in this study and its contribution to optimizing the design and operational efficiency of the dual-stage selective electrodialysis system.
(3) Parameter equations in the manuscript were duplicated in those in the supplementary information, such as the product recovery rate, the total suspended solids measurement, the specific energy consumption.
(4) The e-MCGR process configurations (Lines 418–503) overlap significantly with the membrane stack design and operating/testing descriptions in the supplementary information (Lines 111–193). Redundancy should be minimized.
3. As depicted in FIGURE 4b, the Li2CO3 crystal formed in the base stream loop. However, the method and mechanism to prevent the deposition of Li2CO3 crystals within the membrane stack remain unexplained. Besides, for the in-situ crystallization module, the control strategy of the CO2 inlet flow rate should be clarified. It is recommended to provide a complete device photo.
4. In the line 456 of the manuscript and the line 151 of the supplementary information, the Ksp of Li2CO3 should be about 0.0016 instead of 10^(-10.33).
5. FIGURE S9 shows no permselectivity between Li+ and Ni2+ could not be observed, while the monovalent cation exchange membrane could reject most Ni2+ in Fig3 and FigS8, which is contradictory. The experimental results reflected in Figure S9 should be checked carefully, and the corresponding textual descriptions should be revised to aid readers in comprehending the ideas the authors intend to convey.
6. In line 214-216, the phenomenon of mineral scaling on the membranes at high current density of 5 mA/cm2 was attributed to the poor anti-scaling properties of existing membranes. This explaination is unreasonable. As shown in FIGURE S12, the scaling phenomenon on the surface of the CIMS membrane was more severe than that of the AMX membrane. This should be attributed to the occurrence of water splitting on the surface of CIMS. Due to that most divalent ions are repelled by CIMS and are unable to serve as current carriers, water would be splitted as H+ and OH- to supplement the lack of current carrier flux at the cross section of CIMS, which would be more obvious at high current density.
7. The electro-membrane processes operated at constant current densities. However, neither the manuscript nor the supplementary information reflected any voltage curves of membrane stacks during the operation. These curves are crucial for assessing process stability and concentration polarization. Relevant data and discussion must be added.
8. The influence of the molar ratio of EDTA to Ni2+ and Co2+ was not discussed in the manuscript. However, the molar ratio is a key parameter determining the speciation of Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+ in the wastewater. A lower molar ratio is not conducive to the full conversion of Ni2+ and Co2+ into [EDTA-Ni]2- and [EDTA-Co]2- forms, which in turn is not conducive to the recovery of Ni2+ and Co2+, and will result in the recovered Mn2+ concentrate containing Ni2+ and Co2+ impurities. An excessively high molar ratio will turn part of Mn2+ into [EDTA-Mn]2- form, thereby reducing the recovery rate of Mn2+ and causing the recovered Ni2+ and Co2+ concentrates to contain Mn2+ impurities. Therefore, relevant results and discussion should be supplemented.
9. In FIGURE 5h, the horizontal axes are labeled as "Feed chamber", "Feed chamber", and "Recovery chamber", respectively. However, according to FIGURE S25, they should be "Feed chamber", "Co-extraction chamber", and "Recovery chamber", respectively. Meanwhile, the concentration evolution of Ni2+ and Co2+ in Co-extraction chamber and Recovery chamber was confusing. Within 0 to 10 hours, the concentration of Co2+in the Co-extraction chamber continued to rise, while the concentration of Co2+in the Recovery chamber remained at a low level. This was mainly due to the complexion of Co2+ to Cyanex272 formed the non charged Co(Cyanex272)2. After 10 h, the Co2+ concentration in the Co-extraction chamber declined while that in recovery chamber increased with time. It seemed that H2SO4 was added into the feed solution to substitute Co2+ from Co(Cyanex272)2 (line 184-187 in supplementary information) at the operation time of 10h, but the manuscript did not explicitly clarify this point.
10. FIGURE 5i indicates that the Ni2+ recovery rate at 10h was lower than 80%, but authors claimed that the recovery rate could reach 92.5%. Please provide a reasonable explanation.
11. No feasible method for recycling EDTA and Cyanex 272 was presented or validated. Given their cost and environmental impact, reagent recycling is crucial for the feasibility of divalent ion separation methods.
12. A puzzling phenomenon in economic analysis part is that, as a high-value chemical, Li2CO3 was less profitable than nickel and cobalt compounds in Table S7 and Table S9. Also, the cost of EDTA and Cyanex 272 was ignored in the economic analysis. Authors should clarify these issues and supplement the comparison with mainstream technologies for lithium recovery.
13. In line 226-268 of the supplementary information, the methods of environmental analysis, economic analysis and energy analysis were described vaguely, without necessary data and evaluation methods to support these analysis.
14. The FIGURE 1 in manuscript was not a core content and should not be included in the main text. Also, the cited literature was less relevant to the research content.
15. In line 360-361, authors claimed that "the extra added NaOH and HCl are supplied and reused from the bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization system". It lacked necessary data support from a continuous integrated e-MCGR process.

In addition, in response to the reviewer’s valuable suggestion on “using waste lithium-ion batteries for the experiments”, we have now conducted additional experiments using the real leaching solution derived from spent lithium-ion batteries (see validation of the e-MCGR process using actual LIBs wastewater in methods). The results, now included in the revised manuscript (Fig. 6 and Table S15), show that the Li+ recovery rate approaches 93.6% with product purity > 99.9%. This further validates the effectiveness and applicability of the e-MCGR platform for practical LIB recycling scenarios.
To validate the practical feasibility of the e-MCGR process, real wastewater from spent ternary LIBs is used as feed (Table S15). The spent ternary LIBs, sourced from a technology company's power bank, are used as the primary raw materials. First, 0.4 g of waste NMC111 cathode material is leached in 4.0 M HCl at 80 ºC for 6 h. The resulting leachate is treated by ultrafiltration (UP150 membrane, 0.01 MPa) to remove organic impurities, followed by RO (BW30 membrane, 1.5 MPa) to concentrate the solution. The e-MCGR process for efficient LIBs recycling is further validated using real leachate from spent NMC111 cathode material (Fig. 6a). In the first-stage selective electrodialysis, operated at a current density of 1.0 mA cm−2, the CIMS membranes effectively reject multivalent metal ions (Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+) and permeate monovalent metal ions (Na+ and Li+). Thus, the concentrations of Li+ and Na+ increase to 1.08 g L-1 and 3.73 g L-1 in the recovery chamber, respectively (Fig. 6b). The residual solutions from the transitional chambers (in both transitional chamber-1 and transitional chamber-2) in the first-stage selective electrodialysis are then fed into the second-stage selective electrodialysis for further separation (Fig. 6c). This selective membrane dual-stage distillation configuration achieves accumulative recovery of 93.9% for Li+ and 89.1% for Na+, while completely rejecting Mn2+, Ni2+ and Co2+. This process demonstrated the low energy cost (1.56 $ kg-1), investment cost (7.08 $ kg-1), and energy consumption (14.87 kWh kg-1) (Table S15).
Subsequent bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization process recovers 96.6% Li+ from the leaching solution and produces Li CO with > 99.9% purity (Figs. 6d-e). XPS analysis confirm the product's composition, showing atomic percentages of 32.2% Li, and 39.6% O, with others less than 0.3% (Fig. 6f). The high-purity of 99.9% was further verified by XRD analysis (Fig. 6g). The economic analysis reveals that the primary costs are energy consumption (0.72 $ kg-1 Li CO ) and investment cost (2.12 $ kg-1 Li CO ). Given the current market price of Li CO (24.00 $ kg-1), the system yields a profit of around 21.16 $ kg-1 Li CO (Table S16). Moreover, 97.7% NaOH with 96.7% purity is recovered from the bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization process.
In membrane metal-complexing ex-situ crystallization, due to its lower coordination capacity with EDTA, Mn2+ migrates to the recovery chamber (Fig. 6h). In a separate membrane metal-extracting temporal crystallization step, Ni2+ migrates to the recovery chamber and is recovered as Ni(OH) by adding NaOH (Fig. 6i). With temporal control, the pink Co(OH) is subsequently obtained from the extraction chamber. The membrane metal-complexing ex-situ crystallization proves optimal for maximizing the recovery rate and product purity for all transition metals (Fig. 6j). The XPS spectra results confirm high purity (> 92.0%) of all obtained metal ion products (Fig. 6k). The XRD analysis confirms the generation of Mn O (Fig. 6l). The energy consumption and investment costs are 1.42 and 1.46 $ kg-1 Mn O , respectively. With a market price of ~ 9.00 $ kg-1 Mn O , this configuration yields profits of 6.12 $ kg-1 Mn O (Table S17). XRD analysis confirmed the phase purity of the recovered Ni(OH)₂ and Co(OH)₂ (Figs. 6m-n). The process achieved an 80.1% recovery of Ni(OH)₂ with 99.3% purity and, with temporal control, a 95.6% recovery of pink Co(OH)₂ with 92.2% purity. The combined energy consumption and investment costs for recovering Ni(OH)₂ + Co(OH)₂ are 1.61 and 1.93 $ kg-1 [Ni(OH) + Co(OH) ], respectively. Given market prices of > 14 $ kg-1 for Ni(OH) and > 18 $ kg-1 for Co(OH) , this system brings a profit of 12.58 $ kg-1 [Ni(OH) + Co(OH) ] (Table S18).

4. In Line 201 - 205: A cost of 1.24 $ Kg-1 is reported for Li+ recovery at the first stage (RR = 87.7% at 1.0 mA). When adding the second stage, the cost rose to 2.73 $ Kg– 1. Was the cost of the second stage higher than the first stage, even though the used current density (0.5 mA cm-2) was lower? Also, why did the authors use 0.5 mA? Was it optimized?
Response:
Thank you for your thoughtful questions.
(1) Yes, the cost of the second-stage SED was higher than that of the first stage, despite the lower applied current density (0.5 mA cm⁻²). This is primarily due to two key factors: First, the ion concentration in the feed solution of the second-stage SED was much lower, which resulted in a higher ion migration resistance and thus a higher energy consumption required for ion transport. Second, the lower Li+ concentration in the second-stage feed resulted in a much smaller amount of recovered Li (8.2 kg Y-1) compared to 27.4 kg Y-1 in the first stage. In summary, the higher energy consumption and lower Li recovery amount in the second stage lead to a higher cost of $2.73 kg⁻¹ compared to $1.24 kg⁻¹ in the first stage.
(2) Yes, the current density of 0.5 mA cm-2 was optimized. When selecting the current density in the second-stage SED, we tested the limiting current density of the CIMS membrane using the LIB wastewater, which was determined to be 5.7 mA cm-2. Thus, a low current density of 0.5 mA cm-2 can avoid concentration polarization throughout the process as the concentration of the feed continuously decreases during the experiment. A low current density of 0.5 mA cm-2 is beneficial for Li⁺ with Ni2+, Co2+, and Mn2+.

Methods in the main manuscript:
Pretreatment
The suspended solids in the feed are removed by using ultrafiltration (UP150 membrane) at an operating pressure of 0.01 MPa. Then the permeate is concentrated using reverse osmosis (RO, BW30 membrane) at an operating pressure of 1.5 MPa.
Configurations in the e-MCGR process
All experimental configurations described herein were conducted using a single, consistently prepared complex feed batch (the composition is shown in Supplementary Table S7) to ensure comparability and integration across the e-MCGR process. This batch simulated real LIB leachate and was used sequentially across all experimental stages without intermediate reconstitution. The integrated design of the e-MCGR process comprises:
i. Selective membrane dual-stage distillation configuration: This configuration employs two sequential selective electro-membrane stacks to separate monovalent metal ions (Li+ and Na+) from the divalent metal ions (Mn2+, Ni2+ and Co2+). In the first-stage selective electro-membrane stack (Fig. S6), the membranes are arranged as: anode / bipolar membrane (BM) / AMX (commercial anion exchange membrane) × 3 / CIMS (commercially monovalent cation exchange membrane) × 3 / bipolar membrane (BM) / cathode. The effective area per membrane is 0.0189 m2. Four chambers (feed, transitional-1, transitional-2, recovery) are connected to containers holding 2 L simulated LIB leaching solution in the feed chamber and 0.5 L deionized water in the other chambers. The operational parameters of the current densities are tested at 1 mA cm-2, 2.5 mA cm-2, and 5 mA cm-2. The electric current of the electro-membrane stack is supplied by a stabilized power supply. In order to further distill Li+ and Na+ from transitional chambers (transitional chamber-1 and transitional chamber-2) of the first stage, the second-stage selective electro-membrane stack is developed (Fig. S6), and the electro-membrane stack arrangement is anode / BM / AMX × 2 / CIMS × 2 / BM / cathode. Three chambers in the electro-membrane stack consist of the feed chamber, the transitional chamber, and the recovery chamber. For those chambers, 1 L of residual solution from the first-stage transitional chambers is introduced into the feed chamber of the second-stage stacks, and the transitional and recovery chambers are initially fed with 0.5 L of deionized water. The current density of the electro-membrane stack is 0.5 mA cm-2. The refined Li+ and Na+ from the recovery chamber are then directly used as feed for the subsequent bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization (ii) to separate Li+ from Na+.
ii. Bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization configuration: In this configuration, the electro-membranes are stacked between anode and cathode in a sequence of the anode / BM / AMX / commercial cation exchange membrane (CMX) / BM / cathode (Fig. S13), forming three chambers, including the feed chamber, the acid chamber, and the base chamber. Specifically, 1 L monovalent metal ions solution (Li+ and Na+) from the recovery chambers of configuration (i) is used as the initial feed, and 0.5 L of deionized water is fed to the acid and base chambers. The electric current of this electro-membrane stack is 5 mA cm-2, which is supplied by a direct current-stabilized power supply. To avoid Na+ impurities in Li CO (caused by Na CO co-precipitation) and capture the CO from industry, CO gas is introduced into the base chamber as a carbonate source, at a constant flow rate of 50 mL min-1 (Fig. S14). During the reaction, CO₂ dissolves into the solution and subsequently forms carbonate species. The Li CO crystals will be crystallized in the base solution, followed by Li CO recovery with the UP150 membrane.
iii. Membrane metal-complexing ex-situ crystallization configuration: Here, the membrane sequence is: anode / CMX / AMX / CMX / AMX / cathode (Fig. S19), with three chambers: the feed, complexing, and the recovery chamber. The residual divalent metal-rich solution remaining after configuration (i) serves as the feed for this configuration. Herein, 3.0 L mixtures of Mn2+, Ni2+, and Co2+ are introduced into the feed chamber, and 0.5 L of deionized water is fed into the complexing and recovery chambers.
For the decomplexation, EDTA complexes are dissociated by adding 2.0 M H SO until pH < 0.5. To recover metal ions, Mn2+ in the recovery chamber is precipitated as Mn(OH) by using 2.0 M NaOH. Both the acid and base used here are provided by configuration (ii).
Validation of the e-MCGR process using actual LIBs wastewater
To validate the practical feasibility of the e-MCGR process, real wastewater from spent ternary LIBs is used as feed. The spent ternary LIBs, sourced from a technology company's power bank, are used as the primary raw materials. First, 0.4 g of waste NMC111 cathode material is leached in 4.0 M HCl at 80 ºC for 6 h. The resulting leachate is subjected to the same pretreatment sequence as described in Section “Pretreatment,” namely ultrafiltration (UP150 membrane, 0.01 MPa) to remove organic impurities, followed by RO (BW30 membrane, 1.5 MPa) to concentrate the solution. The concentrated leachate, now enriched in Li⁺, Na⁺, Mn²⁺, Ni²⁺, and Co²⁺, is directly used as the feed for the e-MCGR process, without reconstitution or modification, to ensure a one-to-one comparison with the results obtained from the simulated LIB leachate.

Zhao and his colleagues reported a combined electro-membrane crystallization
process for spent lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) recycling, termed e-MCGR technology.
The proposed technology incorporated four core modules: selective membrane dual-
stage distillation, bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization, membrane metal-
complexing ex-situ crystallization, and membrane metal-extracting temporal
crystallization. However, similar individual module technologies have been proposed
by peers for the recycling of lithium and other metallic elements from LIB streams
(AIChE J. 68(2022), 17710; Nature Water 1(2023) 547-554; Chemical Engineering
Journal 348(2018) 952-959; Resources, Conservation & Recycling 178 (2022) 106076;
et al.). (1) The novelty of this system is not clear because this article merely
conceptually integrates these modular technologies. (2) Furthermore, the above
modules were studied separately in this manuscript, resulting in weak interconnectivity
among them and insufficient comprehensive examination of the overall practical
feasibility of the integrated technology. (3) Additionally, the discussion on selective
electrodialysis, electro-driven membrane in-situ crystallization and metal-extracting
crystallization was insufficient, with some principal explanations containing scientific
errors. (4) The research results are insufficient to demonstrate the practical feasibility
of the proposed e-MCGR technology. Therefore, this paper is not suitable for
publication in Nature Communications. The detailed comments are as follows.

valuable feedback provided. We understand and respect the reviewer’s concerns

these as an independent process. The novelty and significance of our study lie in: 1)
as we mentioned in the introduction, the e-MCGR process is purposely designed to
address both separation precision and practical applicability by sequentially
integrating membrane crystallization, metal extraction, and metal complexation
modules. This integration enables stepwise separation of Li⁺, Na⁺, Mn²⁺, Ni²⁺, and Co²⁺

viability alongside technical performance, providing a more complete assessment of
industrial applicability. 3) Moreover, we have conducted additional experiments using

the revised manuscript, further validate the effectiveness and applicability of the

addressed and validated in previous studies.

functionally relevant in conventional CIMS applications, specify the primary
mechanism governing the CIMS in this study and its contribution to optimizing the
design and operational efficiency of the dual-stage selective electrodialysis system.
Response:
Thanks for your valuable comment. We have revised the manuscript to make it clear.
“Previously, membrane technologies have relied on principles such as size exclusion,
electrostatic interactions, and chemical affinity to achieve ion selectivity.31,40-42
Although substantial progress has been made toward developing membranes with
precise single-ion selectivity, their utility in real-world resource recovery remains
limited by material constraints and has largely been tested only in isolated/single
systems.43-45 Furthermore, their applicability in LIB recycling has not been convincingly
demonstrated.”
The mechanisms for preparing electro-driven membrane with ion selectivity mainly
include membrane pore size sieving, electrostatic repulsion, and chemical affinity.
Based on the characteristics of the commercial CIMS used in this study:
The primary ion sieving mechanisms of CIMS are identified as electrostatic repulsion
and size sieving. The polyamino compound layer grafted on the CIMS surface
introduces abundant amino groups, imparting positive charges to the membrane
surface. This positively charged layer strongly repels multivalent cations such as Ni²⁺,
Co²⁺, and Mn²⁺, while monovalent cations (e.g., Na⁺, Li⁺) with lower charge density
experience much weaker repulsion, enabling preferential transport (Fig. S5a). In
addition, the relatively dense structure of the CIMS membrane matrix provides a size
sieving effect, where Na⁺ and Li⁺, with smaller hydrated radii, permeate more easily
than the larger hydrated Ni2+, Co2+, and Mn2+ (Fig. S5b). The synergy between
electrostatic repulsion and size sieving enhances monovalent selectivity, thereby
contributing to the optimized design and operational efficiency of the dual-stage
selective electrodialysis system. The potential mechanism could be the chemical
affinity, which relates to chemical interactions between molecules, ions, or compounds.
In membrane separation processes, the chemical affinity is the tendency of molecules,
ions, or compounds to chemically interact with active groups within the membrane or
on the membrane surface. The most important chemical interaction between these
species is bonding and is described by bonding affinity. As shown in Fig. S5c, under
the influence of a driving force, molecules, ions, or compounds with higher
chemical/binding affinity (f ) to the membrane structure will more readily interact with
ca
the membrane surface and transport across the membrane. In contrast, ions with a
higher mass transfer resistance will not be able to cross the membrane surface and
are selectively retained.
Supplementary Figure S5. The mechanisms of commercial monovalent ion-selective
electro-membranes. (a) Electrostatic repulsion; (b) Size exclusion; (c) Chemical affinity.
More detail information had been published in our previous work:
Zhao, Y. et al. Advanced ion transfer materials in electro-driven membrane processes
for sustainable ion-resource extraction and recovery. Prog. Mater. Sci. 128, 100958
(2022).

6. In line 214-216, the phenomenon of mineral scaling on the membranes at high
current density of 5 mA/cm2 was attributed to the poor anti-scaling properties of
existing membranes. This explanation is unreasonable. As shown in FIGURE S12, the
scaling phenomenon on the surface of the CIMS membrane was more severe than
that of the AMX membrane. This should be attributed to the occurrence of water
splitting on the surface of CIMS. Due to that most divalent ions are repelled by CIMS
and are unable to serve as current carriers, water would be splitted as H+ and OH- to
supplement the lack of current carrier flux at the cross section of CIMS, which would
be more obvious at high current density.
Response:
Thanks for your critical observation. We agree that the previous attribution to the poor
anti-scaling properties of the membranes was incomplete. Due to the polyamino
compound layer on the CIMS surface enhances electrostatic repulsion, an ion
concentration gradient forms in the boundary layer. Although the operating current
density was below the measured limiting current density, the reduced ion
concentration in the boundary layer will elevate ion depletion, creating a localized
micro-environment where ion transport is imbalanced. Consequently, water molecules
in the boundary layer undergo forced ionization to generate H⁺ and OH⁻ for charge
compensation. The OH- reacts with accumulated metal ions to form insoluble
hydroxide precursors for membrane scaling formation (Fig. S13).
We revised the explanation of scaling in the manuscript and provided a schematic
illustration of the scaling phenomenon in the supplementary materials:
“While selective membrane dual-stage distillation technology achieves a high
separation efficiency, current commercial membranes are limited by their metal ion
throughput. In addition, they suffer from severe membrane scaling (Fig. S11 and Fig.
S12). On the one hand, this scaling can be attributed to the inherent poor anti-scaling
properties of commercial electro-membrane. On the other hand, water splitting may
occur on the CIMS surface as most divalent ions are electrostatically repelled and
cannot serve as current carriers. The resulting shortage of charge carriers induces
forced dissociation of water into H⁺ and OH⁻, with OH⁻ reacting with accumulated
metal ions to form insoluble hydroxide precursors that deposit on the membrane
surface (Fig. S13).”

7. The electro-membrane processes operated at constant current densities. However,
neither the manuscript nor the supplementary information reflected any voltage curves
of membrane stacks during the operation. These curves are crucial for assessing
process stability and concentration polarization. Relevant data and discussion must
be added.
Response:
Thanks for your suggestions. Relevant data and discussion have been added in Fig.
S9 in the Supplementary Information.
Fig. S9 illustrates the voltage drop changes for the multi-stage selective electrodialysis
operations. The voltage drop across the selective electrodialysis stack changes
smoothly during the operation, which indicates the constant migration of ions through
ion exchange membranes at different stages. The voltage drop at the ends of both
selective electrodialysis stacks increased with an increase in current density, followed
by a decrease and stabilization (Figs. S9b-c). According to Ohm’s law, at a constant
current density, higher resistance leads to a higher voltage. At the beginning of the
experiment, ions entering the concentration chamber through the CIMS membrane
and AMX membrane cause the resistance of the membrane stack to decrease.
Subsequently, ions migrate steadily to adjacent chambers, keeping the resistance of
the membrane stack almost constant. The passage of Li⁺ and blocking of Ni²⁺, Co²⁺,
and Mn²⁺ occur gradually under the action of the electric field, resulting in the voltage
drop first decreasing and then stabilizing.
In the bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization system, the voltage drop initially
exhibited a higher value due to the elevated resistance caused by deionized water in
the acid/base chambers (Fig. S9d). Subsequently, the bipolar membrane generated
H⁺/OH⁻, which combined with anions/cations from the feed chamber to form acid/base,
leading to a stable voltage trend. In the later stage of the experiment, a large number
of ions were transferred from the feed chamber, causing the resistance of the feed
chamber to become a major contributor to the overall stack resistance; consequently,
the membrane stack resistance increased rapidly. As a result, the voltage of the
membrane stack rose sharply in the later stages of the experiment.
In complexation electrodialysis, the chelated species formed after chelation with
divalent transition metal ions in the leachate exist as anionic species ([EDTA-Co]²⁻
and [EDTA-Ni]²⁻) (Fig. S9e). Similarly, the voltage drop initially decreases, then
stabilizes, and finally increases. At the beginning of the experiment, [EDTA-Co]²⁻ and
[EDTA-Ni]²⁻ ions migrate into the complexing chamber through the CMX membrane,
while Mn²⁺ ions enter the recovery chamber through the AMX membrane; these
processes collectively lead to a decrease in the membrane stack resistance.
Subsequently, ions migrate steadily into adjacent chambers, maintaining the
membrane stack resistance at an almost constant level. In the later stage of the
experiment, the depletion of ions in the feed chamber causes its resistance to increase
rapidly.
In the membrane-based metal-extracting temporal crystallization system, the voltage
initially exhibited a higher value due to the presence of deionized water in the Ni-
recovery chamber at the start of the experiment. Under the applied electric field, Ni²⁺
and Co²⁺ ions then migrated into the extraction chamber through the CMX membrane,
leading to a decrease in the membrane stack resistance (Fig. S9f). Within this process,
Co²⁺ was extracted by Cyanex 272, while Ni²⁺ continued to migrate into the Ni-recovery
chamber through the CMX membrane. Subsequently, ions transferred steadily to
adjacent chambers, maintaining the membrane stack resistance at an almost constant
level. Finally, as the ion concentration in the feed chamber became low, the voltage of
the system showed an increasing trend.

electrodialysis, (c) second-stage selective electrodialysis, (d) bipolar membrane in-situ
crystallization system, (e) complexation electrodialysis, and (f) membrane metal-

Response: Thanks for your comment. To address this, we provide the detailed
methodologies for environmental analysis, economic analysis, and energy analysis in
the supplementary materials. Moreover, to make this analysis more robust and clear
in the revised manuscript, we will supplement specific data to support these claims.
(1) Economic analysis: An economic analysis is important for assessing the potential of the
integrated system for achieving near zero discharge from spent LIBs wastewater. The overall
recovery cost for spent LIBs wastewater contained energy cost and investment cost. The
lifetime of the integrated system device was set as three years and relied on lab-scale data.
In pilot plant tests and industrial-scale operations, fixed costs were amortized as production
volume increased, reducing unit costs and enhancing economic attractiveness. The optimized
e-MCGR process achieves a recovery of 95.5% for Li+, 99.5% for Mn2+, 83.1% for Ni2+, and
87.3% for Co2+, yielding high product purities of 99.9% for Li CO , 99.9% for Mn O , 99.5%
2 3 3 4

scale also enhanced operational efficiency and by-product utilization, such as promoting
Li CO , Ni(OH) , Co(OH) , and Mn O recovery and reducing energy consumption, which
2 3 2 2 3 4
positively impacted the economic viability of the project. The economic analysis is calculated
according to the method in Table S10.
(2) Energy analysis: From an energy consumption perspective, although the
electrodialysis process requires electrical energy, the overall energy balance is
favorable when considering the value of the recovered metals. When evaluating the
overall energy balance, it is essential to consider the energy savings achieved by
avoiding primary metal mining. The extraction of lithium, nickel, cobalt, and
manganese from the natural ores is an extremely energy-intensive process. It involves
activities such as ore mining, crushing, grinding, and complex chemical separation
processes. By recycling these metals from spent LIBs wastewater through integrated
electrodialysis technology, a significant amount of energy consumed in primary mining
can be saved. In addition, the energy efficiency of the electrodialysis integrated system
can be further improved through process optimization. The adjustment of operating
parameters, such as current density, to achieve a higher crystallization rate with the
lowest energy input. The optimized e-MCGR process achieves an energy
consumption of 11.83 kWh kg-1 for the first-stage selective electrodialysis, an energy
consumption of 15.97 kWh kg-1 for the second-stage selective electrodialysis, an
energy consumption of 10.45 kWh kg-1 for the bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization
system, and an energy consumption of 17.96 kWh kg-1 for the membrane metal-
complexing ex-situ crystallization and membrane metal-extracting temporal
crystallization. Moreover, the possible integration of renewable energy sources will be
useful. For example, solar or wind power can be used to supply part of the electrical
energy required for the integrated electrodialysis process, which not only reduces the
reliance on traditional fossil fuel-based energy but also further improves the overall
energy sustainability of the metal recycling process. Thus, our method shows great
potential in terms of energy efficiency and sustainability.
(3) Environmental analysis: The environmental analysis in this study is conducted
through a comparison between traditional processes (e.g., pyrometallurgy and
hydrometallurgy) and the e-MCGR technology. This focuses on highlighting the
environmental benefits of the e-MCGR technology of spent LIBs wastewater recovery.
The details are as follows: The implementation of electro-driven membrane technology
significantly reduces the environmental burden associated with the disposal of spent
LIBs wastewater. Traditional disposal methods (e.g., pyrometallurgy and
hydrometallurgy) often lead to the release of heavy metals (such as nickel, cobalt, and
manganese) into the environment, which will cause soil and water pollution. However,
extra reagent consumption, significant waste emission, secondary pollutant
generation and complicated separation routes are limited. By recovering valuable
elements (i.e., Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+) through electro-driven membrane technology, the
potential for environmental contamination is greatly mitigated. This not only aligns with
the principles of the circular economy but also reduces the volume of waste that needs
to be disposed of in landfills. The sustainable membrane-based technologies promote
the development of environmentally friendly strategies in the battery industry.

All experimental configurations described herein were conducted using a single,
consistently prepared complex feed batch (the composition is shown in Supplementary
Table S7) to ensure comparability and integration across the e-MCGR process. This
batch simulated real LIB leachate and was used sequentially across all experimental
stages without intermediate reconstitution (Table S19). The integrated design of the
e-MCGR process comprises:
i. Selective membrane dual-stage distillation configuration: This configuration employs
two sequential selective electro-membrane stacks to separate monovalent metal ions
(Li+ and Na+) from the divalent metal ions (Mn2+, Ni2+ and Co2+). In the first-stage
selective electro-membrane stack (Fig. S6), the membranes are arranged as: anode /
bipolar membrane (BM) / AMX (commercial anion exchange membrane) × 3 / CIMS
(commercially monovalent cation exchange membrane) × 3 / bipolar membrane (BM)
/ cathode (Table S20). The effective area per membrane is 0.0189 m2. Four chambers
(feed, transitional-1, transitional-2, recovery) are connected to containers holding 2 L
simulated LIB leaching solution in the feed chamber and 0.5 L deionized water in the
other chambers. The operational parameters of the current densities are tested at 1
mA cm-2, 2.5 mA cm-2, and 5 mA cm-2. The electric current of the electro-membrane
stack is supplied by a stabilized power supply. In order to further distill Li+ and Na+
from transitional chambers (transitional chamber-1 and transitional chamber-2) of the
first stage, the second-stage selective electro-membrane stack is developed (Fig. S6),
and the electro-membrane stack arrangement is anode / BM / AMX × 2 / CIMS × 2 /
BM / cathode. Three chambers in the electro-membrane stack consist of the feed
chamber, the transitional chamber, and the recovery chamber. For those chambers, 1
L of residual solution from the first-stage transitional chambers is introduced into the
feed chamber of the second-stage stacks, and the transitional and recovery chambers
are initially fed with 0.5 L of deionized water. The current density of the electro-
membrane stack is 0.5 mA cm-2. The refined Li+ and Na+ from the recovery chamber
are then directly used as feed for the subsequent bipolar membrane in-situ
crystallization (ii) to separate Li+ from Na+.
ii. Bipolar membrane in-situ crystallization configuration: In this configuration, the
electro-membranes are stacked between anode and cathode in a sequence of the
anode / BM / AMX / commercial cation exchange membrane (CMX) / BM / cathode
(Fig. S13), forming three chambers, including the feed chamber, the acid chamber,
and the base chamber. Specifically, 1 L monovalent metal ions solution (Li+ and Na+)
from the recovery chambers of configuration (i) is used as the initial feed, and 0.5 L of
deionized water is fed to the acid and base chambers. The electric current of this
electro-membrane stack is 5 mA cm-2, which is supplied by a direct current-stabilized
power supply. To avoid Na+ impurities in Li CO (caused by Na CO co-precipitation)

To validate the practical feasibility of the e-MCGR process, real wastewater from spent
ternary LIBs is used as feed. The spent ternary LIBs, sourced from a technology
company's power bank, are used as the primary raw materials. First, 0.4 g of waste
NMC111 cathode material is leached in 4.0 M HCl at 80 ºC for 6 h. The resulting
leachate is subjected to the same pretreatment sequence as described in Section
“Pretreatment,” namely ultrafiltration (UP150 membrane, 0.01 MPa) to remove organic
impurities, followed by RO (BW30 membrane, 1.5 MPa) to concentrate the solution.
The concentrated leachate, now enriched in Li⁺, Na⁺, Mn²⁺, Ni²⁺, and Co²⁺, is directly
used as the feed for the e-MCGR process, without reconstitution or modification, to
ensure a one-to-one comparison with the results obtained from the simulated LIB
leachate.
